story.en: Yuna Kim is finishing dinner when a work message appears at 9:14 p.m. Her manager asks for a quick answer, but Yuna promised herself a quiet evening with her sister. Last month, a teammate who ignored late messages missed an important update. Her sister jokes that the phone deserves its own chair. Yuna must decide whether to reply now, set a boundary, or wait until morning.

page2.title: Why Cities Are Rethinking Public Benches

source.title: Cities debate the future of public seating
source.excerpt: A report on how public benches affect rest, access and the way people use shared streets.

page2.article: Public benches may look like small pieces of street furniture, but they shape who can comfortably use a neighbourhood. Older adults, parents, commuters and people with disabilities often rely on a place to pause. Some cities remove benches to discourage long stays, while others add them to make public spaces more welcoming. Supporters say good seating encourages walking and chance conversations. Critics worry about maintenance costs and misuse. The debate asks whether a city should design its streets mainly for moving through or for spending time together.
